summary: Help 6-7 year olds grasp the inverse-size relationship: cutting the SAME whole into more equal shares makes each share smaller. A quarter of a pizza is a smaller amount than a half of the same pizza, and an eighth smaller still. This directly confronts the whole-number bias by which children read a bigger denominator as a bigger amount ('4 > 2 so a quarter is bigger'). When comparing the actual amounts, the comparison relies on the wholes being identical, and it seeds later unit-fraction comparison (1/3 > 1/4).
misconceptions: Larger denominator = larger fraction / whole-number bias ('a quarter is bigger than a half because 4 is more than 2'; 1/8 > 1/3) - documented in IES
Comparing fractions of DIFFERENT-sized wholes without noticing the whole matters
Confusing the number of pieces with the amount in one piece ('4 pieces is more than 2 pieces')

activities.title: Predict-then-check with two identical pizzas
steps: Give the child two identical paper 'pizzas' of exactly the same size (the paper stands in for the flat region being shared - what matters is the amount each piece represents, not the paper itself).
Before cutting, ask them to predict: if one pizza is cut into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4 equal pieces, whose single piece will be bigger, and why? Record the stated reason.
Cut both pizzas and lay one half on top of one quarter so the child can see the half blankets the quarter with room to spare.
Then cut (or imagine cutting) the same-size whole into 8, then more, and have the child watch a single piece keep getting smaller.
Name the pattern out loud together: 'more equal shares of the same whole means smaller pieces.'
activities.insight: A single share gets smaller as the same whole is split among more sharers, so a half of a pizza is a bigger amount than a quarter of the same pizza even though 4 is more than 2.

activities.title: Live share-slider: watch one piece shrink
steps: Show two identical circular pizzas side by side, each with a control that sets the number of equal shares.
Have the child set one pizza to 2 shares and the other to 4, highlight one piece on each, then drag the highlighted pieces together to overlay them.
Ask the child to describe what happens to the overlapped pieces: the half covers the quarter with space left over.
Have the child push the share control higher (8, 10, 12) on one pizza and describe how a single highlighted piece keeps shrinking.
activities.insight: As the number of equal shares rises, one share visibly shrinks, making the inverse relationship between number of shares and size of each share concrete.

activities.title: Order and compare unit fractions of the same whole
steps: Show pictures of 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/8 of the SAME cake and ask the child to order them largest to smallest.
Ask the child to explain why the order goes that way in terms of sharing.
Ask the child directly: 'Why doesn't the biggest number on the bottom mean the biggest piece?'
Pose a comparison question such as: 'Who has more, someone with a half of a cake or someone with a quarter of the same cake?' and ask for the reason.
Ask the trap question: 'Could a quarter ever be a bigger amount than a half? What would have to be true about the two cakes?'
activities.insight: Unit fractions of the same whole can be ordered by size (1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/8); when comparing the actual amounts in the pieces, the comparison relies on the wholes being the same size.

activities.title: Aligned fraction wall as a reference
steps: Show a fraction wall with rows for 1 whole, halves, quarters and eighths, all aligned to the same total length.
Have the child point to and compare a single tile in each row against the whole and against each other.
Ask them to find which single tile is biggest and which is smallest, and to say why.
activities.insight: A single piece gets shorter as the whole is divided into more equal parts, shown against a common length.

checkQuestion: Two children each have a whole pizza, exactly the same size. Ali cuts hers into 2 equal pieces and takes one piece. Bea cuts hers into 4 equal pieces and takes one piece. Ask: 'Who has more pizza to eat - and how do you know?' Then ask: 'Why does cutting the same pizza into MORE pieces make each piece smaller?'
checkAnswer: Ali has more - a half is bigger than a quarter of the same pizza. Cutting the same whole into more equal pieces makes each piece smaller, because one whole is being shared among more parts. (Tier 2: the more sharers, the less each one gets.)
